articleTitle: A few notes on oversea wireless stations heard in Johannesburg
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The question of the successful reception of overseas high-powered transmitting stations should not be one of difficulty to the serious experimenter, and at times it is a less difficult proposition than that of receiving some of our local coast and ships' stations. The power at the hack of the larger Continental and American stations is such that with suitable coils and a valve, little difficulty, if any, should be experienced in satisfactorily reading them at any time of the day, provided, of course, that atmospheric conditions are good. Quite a number of the stations send at a very moderate rate, and the experimenter who is able to read fifteen words a minute should be able to take down such work, especially as in most eases each word is repeated. This offers a splendid opportunity to the keen worker to increase his morse-reading ability. It seems somewhat incomprehensible that anyone can derive any great enjoyment from listening to a meaningless jumble of sounds, and, furthermore, not even knowing from which part of the globe the signals emanate. At various times details of minor occurrences have been noted, which, although of only minute importance, are yet interesting to a degree to the keen observer.

articleTitle: Progressive lightning
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A method of obtaining direct information as to the mode of development of the lightning discharge has been described by Boys.<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup> it consists in the use of a camera with a fixed plate and two lenses revolving in a circle at opposite ends of a diameter. The two pictures of the lightning flash thus obtained show distortions, due to the motions of the lenses, which are in opposite directions. From a comparison of the two pictures and a knowledge of the velocities of the lenses, it is possible to deduce the direction and speed of the developing discharge.

articleTitle: The development of the lightning discharge
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: We should like to give a brief account of some further results obtained with the Boys lightning camera, which has now been modified so as to include a means of determining the order of the component strokes of a discharge. The material available refers to 55 lightning flashes from eleven different thunderstorms, and the total number of separate strokes photographed is 145. Of these, 65 show clearly the two-fold character which we have previously reported, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1,2</sup> namely, it downward-moving leader stroke which at the moment it strikes the ground causes the development of a faster and more intense upward-moving main stroke. If we exclude those strokes photographed under definitely bad conditions (too great a distance, obscured by rain, etc.), the fraction of the strokes showing the leader mechanism is raised from 45 per cent. (65/143) to 82 per cent. (41/50). Similarly, while 62 per cent. (34/55) of the separate flashes show one or more examples of leaders, the percentage is raised to 86 per cent, (18/21) if we consider the better photographs only.

The matter was brought up in some constructional features of the new Capetown broadcasting station, recently commissioned. As in the latest practice in telephonic transmission, this station has a very flexible system of combining the amplification stages; a system of “jacks” being arranged on a panel whereby any set Of, say, microphone amplifiers may be connected to any one “A” amplifier” in much the same way as a telephone operator connects two subscribers.

articleTitle: “An analysis of the lightning faulting characteristics of the 132 kv lines of the victoria falls and transvaal power company, limited.”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I should like to join in congratulating the authors of this important paper and the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Company on the achievement of a very notable piece of work. It is notable not only for the fact that it deals with lightning faulting in a region which can hardly he inferior to any part of the world in its susceptibility to lightning, but also because it employs for the first time a new, direct and most powerful method for the study of the subject. And, finally, it is notable for the skill with which the authors have exploited this method to obtain the last ounce of information from the records at their disposal. The result is a most satisfying and conclusive demonstration of the chief cause of double line faulting and of the means by which such faulting can be minimised.

articleTitle: Valedictory address

The twenty-four years' record of the Institute, with its outstanding roll of Past Presidents, is one of enthusiasm, progress and energy, and the good name of the Institute to-day stands high, not only among the technical associations of South Africa, but in many of the overseas countries which take an interest in its work and publications.

articleTitle: Earth leakage protection at daggafontein mines, ltd. — The installation and its operating results
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Before proceeding with a description of the earth leakage equipment, as installed at Daggafontein Mines, Ltd., it is felt that, as this mine was the first on these fields to put this form of protection into general use for its electrical system, a brief review of the principles and merits of earth leakage protection in general would not be out of place, although these are possibly well well known to many. This form of protection is based on the fact that in any system of conductors transmitting three-phase electrical energy, whether an overhead line or cable, the instantaneous vectorial sum of the currents in the conductors of that System is zero. This balance would, however, be upset should a fault develop in the system concerned in such a way that portion of the current returns via some other conductor, generally the earth, to its source of generation or transformation. It is this out of balance current, or rather its effect, which is made use of to trip the faulty circuit.

articleTitle: Contemporary advances in sub-atomic chemistry
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, I shall endeavour to make the discussion as simple as possible, my object being to bring to the notice of the members of The South African Institute of Electrical Engineers the present position as regards the structure of the atom, and more particularly the recent work in connection with the structure of the nucleus. It is my intention to trace the historical development of the earlier conceptions of the electron, the proton and alpha particle and the more recent particles, the neutron, positive electron and the deuton. From the latter I will move the discussion to the new hydrogen and its compounds, in particular heavy water. I shall endeavour to show how the recent investigations on the nucleus led to the discovery of the hydrogen isotopes, and subsequently to the discovery of heavy water and the interesting properties of the latter will be mentioned.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Alternating Current is now almost universally adopted as the most convenient form of electrical energy for all industrial purposes. In spite of its increasing use, there are nevertheless many instances where Direct Current is either essential or preferable. For electrolysis, certain chemical processes, battery charging, and D.C. Traction, it is essential, and where wide and economical speed control of motors is desirable D.C. still holds its own despite the variable speed A.C. commutator motor which is available in the smaller sizes. Some form of converting or rectifying plant is, therefore, necessary to change the A.C. supply into D.C.

abstract: (Contribution received from the Publicity Department of the South African Railways and Harbours.) Those who are contemplating a holiday this spring or summer and desire a change from the hustle of the larger resorts, those in search of a quiet place beside the sea, a haven of rest and recreation, a natural beauty spot on river bank or seashore where all the worries and troubles of every-day existence are forgotten amidst surroundings of distinctive natural appeal, and where the call to healthful outdoor life is irresistible, will find their requirements met, however exacting be their taste, at any of the resorts taken at random and described below. On the picturesque Garden Route in the South-Western Cape, and some twenty miles from Knysna, is Plettenberg Bay, a deep inlet protected by Cape Seal. The coastline provides many vantage points from which magnificent sea-scapes can be viewed, while the beach, which curves round for a distance of about two miles to the mouth of the beautiful Keurbooms River offers good bathing.

articleTitle: Symmetrical components (appendix)
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Single Phase Oscillating Field. Any single phase field with its axis fixed in space may be regarded as made up of two D.C. fields rotating synchronously in opposite directions, and having equal magnitudes. The magnitude of each of these fields is half that of the maximum value of the single phase field. This is illustrated by Fig. 25a. If we represent the D.C. fields by permanent magnets, rotating as shown, then at the instant when like poles coincide, the resultant field will have a maximum value vertically (i.e., twice that of one D.C. field). After a quarter revolution unlike poles coincide, and the resultant vertical field will be zero. After a further quarter revolution like poles again coincide, and the resultant vertical field will again be a maximum, but in the opposite sense.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A Specification for insulating boards and tubes made from paper or paper-pulp treated with synthetic resin and bonded together under the influence of heat and pressure was issued in 1929 as British Standard Specification No. 316. That specification was, however, limited to Grade 11 material, which is suitable for use on oil-immersed apparatus and on low-voltage apparatus working in air in dry situations. For certain purposes, however, such as the insulation of apparatus working in humid atmospheres, and for the production of components by machining operations, a different grade of the same class of material is required, and this (higher) grade is now covered by the recently-issued B.S. Specification for Grade I Synthetic-resin Bonded-paper Sheets for Electrical Purposes (B.S.S. No. 547–1934). Grade I material is distinguished from Grade II material by low water absorption, high resistivity, low dielectric loss and good machining properties. It is known commercially under such trade names as pascolin, tufuol, bakelite, etc., and is used extensively for the insulation of telephone switch-boards, armature wedges, terminal strips, armature tooth supports, etc.

abstract: Mr. Janovsky, in his discussion on the paper read by the authors before the Institute in August, 1933, proffered some interesting remarks on the precautions to be taken, and the most suitable instruments to be used, when making mercury-arc rectifier measurements.

articleTitle: The Jeppe street power station of the city of Johannesburg electricity undertaking
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: At the outset of my comments I wish to congratulate the author on his paper, which not only deals in an interesting manner with some of the difficulties encountered in the operation of the Jeppe Street Station, but also brings into prominence various costs which go to make up the total production cost of electricity.

articleTitle: Annual Banquet
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The Council of the Institute is indebted ! to the Editor of the Rand Daily Mail for permission to reproduce the newspaper report of the Institute's Annual Banquet.

articleTitle: The electrical equipment of the South African iron and steel industrial corporation, limited
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The establishment of a comprehensive iron and steel industry on modern lines in this country has brought with it a number of engineering problems which are new to South Africa. The intention of this paper is to present a general description of the electrical equipment of the South African Iron and Steel Industrial Corporation, Ltd., and to examine some, of the more unusual electrical problems encountered during the layout, construction and starting up periods.

articleTitle: Test results from camera records
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: My thanks are due to this Institution for their invitation to read this paper, which is a sequel to the paper read before it in 1929 by Mr. L. B. Woodworth, a pioneer in respect of many things electrical.

articleTitle: Electro magnetic waves
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I have to thank Mr. Everett very much for inviting me to contribute to the discussion on his very interesting and able paper on “Electro Magnetic Waves” and the earth's electric field and the unsolved problems associated with this.

articleTitle: Phase sequence and symmetrical components in alternating current systems
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This paper is an attempt to explain the use of symmetrical components in analysing three-phase systems of currents and voltages. A few particular cases will be outlined, and some test results given in order to illustrate the ideas involved. The methods employed will be described in detail, and difficulties arising in the practical application of the theory will be considered. Reference will also be made to some protection devices, the functioning of which can be explained by the use of symmetrical components. It might be mentioned here that the ideas of symmetrical component analysis were originally introduced by Mr: C. L. Fortescue in America in 1918.

articleTitle: Problems of artifical illumination
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: To all who are interested in the subject of illumination, a brief survey of the early times forms a fitting background from which remarkable changes of the last three centuries stand out with great vividness.
